\title{Epistemic Hedging is Linear in Pretrained Sentence Embeddings}

\author{Anonymous Submission \\
  \texttt{anonymized@example.com}}

\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Epistemic hedging --- words like ``probably,'' ``certainly,'' and ``possibly'' --- has been psychometrically calibrated since the 1960s, with median probabilities for verbal expressions remarkably stable across more than fifty years of replication. We investigate whether this calibration is recoverable as a \textbf{verbal probability axis} in frozen pretrained pooled sentence embeddings. Within syntactic types, verbal probability is the dominant linear direction across five architecturally diverse embedding models (supervised Spearman \(\rho > 0.90\)), and the axis triangulates against two independent psychometric datasets at \(\rho \approx 0.97\) in both. The same axis transfers in ranking across eight typologically diverse languages via a multilingual encoder, is robust to an order of magnitude of dimensional compression on a Matryoshka-trained model, and passes permutation and label-shuffling null tests on the three larger-\(n\) syntactic types. Rank-1 representation-level erasure of the axis clears two complementary nulls --- a cosine-matched random-direction control and a label-permutation null --- at \(p = 0.002\) on the headline cross-type pair across two architectures, the embedding-class structural analogue of activation-steering experiments standard in the decoder-LLM linear-feature literature. We frame the empirical convergence across three psychometric datasets, six embedding architectures, and eight languages as evidence that distributional embedding geometry and human probability semantics are convergent measurements of one underlying epistemic dimension.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{introduction}

\citet{mikolov2013linguistic} demonstrated that semantic relationships manifest as consistent vector directions in word embedding space --- \emph{king − man + woman ≈ queen}. The Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) generalizes this observation: many human-meaningful concepts correspond to linear directions in language model representations \citep{park2024linear}. Three lines of recent work bear on whether epistemic content fits this pattern.

\textbf{Linear features in decoder LLM internal states.} \citet{marks2023geometry} identify a truth direction in residual stream activations. \citet{burger2024truth} refine truth representations to handle polarity confounds. \citet{yu2025directions} generalize one-dimensional truth directions to multi-dimensional cones. \citet{ji2025calibrating} identify a single linear ``verbal uncertainty'' feature in residual streams that can be causally manipulated to reduce overconfident hallucinations. \citet{lepori2026fantasy} link decoder hidden-state directions to graded human plausibility and modal judgments. \citet{valois2025frame} extend single-token concept directions to multi-token ``frames'' via the Frame Representation Hypothesis, with steering experiments on the unembedding matrix. All of these works share a methodological commitment: they study internal states of decoder LLMs --- residual streams, unembedding matrices, layer-wise activations --- where token-level causal intervention (steering, activation patching) is natural because the model generates tokens.

\textbf{Verbal-probability psychometrics elicited behaviorally from language models.} A parallel literature studies how language models interpret hedge expressions like ``likely,'' ``probably,'' and ``possibly'' by \emph{prompting} the model and comparing its outputs to human numerical judgments. \citet{sileo2023probing} probe pretrained models for words-of-estimative-probability classification (with fine-tuning). \citet{belem2024perceptions} compare LLM and human numerical interpretations of linguistic uncertainty expressions through prompted-output protocols. \citet{tang2026evaluation} extend this to multilingual estimative uncertainty. \citet{wang2024calibrating} calibrate certainty-phrase distributions using transport-based methods. These papers establish that verbal probability semantics are recoverable from language models \emph{behaviorally}, but they do not extract a geometric structure from frozen embedding representations.

\textbf{Pretrained sentence embedding probing for human-aligned graded properties.} A third line studies pooled sentence representations directly. Most directly relevant: \citet{jacobs2022masked} probe mean-pooled RoBERTa sentence embeddings for human cloze-based uncertainty (next-word predictability and sentential constraint), demonstrating that pooled embedding spaces encode some form of human-aligned uncertainty. \citet{chen2019uncertain} show that fine-tuned BERT-based regressors can predict continuous human probability judgments in sentence-pair NLI. \citet{schuster2019harnessing} predict human scalar pragmatic ratings from sentence encoders. \citet{pei2021measuring} regress continuous certainty in scientific writing. These works establish that pooled sentence embeddings carry \emph{some} graded epistemic content --- but for cloze probability, NLI inference strength, or rhetorical certainty rather than verbal probability semantics, and not as a frozen-geometry linear axis calibrated against psychometric data.

\textbf{The gap.} No prior work has demonstrated a \emph{continuously calibrated verbal probability axis} in \emph{frozen pretrained pooled sentence embeddings}, \emph{aligned with human psychometric judgments} and \emph{validated against independent psychometric datasets}. We address this gap. We use the \citet{mosteller1990quantifying} dataset, which provides empirically calibrated probability distributions for 53 verbal expressions (e.g., ``likely'' → median 71.1\%, ``possible'' → median 38.5\%) collected from 238 science writers. We embed these in controlled sentence templates, extract difference vectors from bare claims, and test whether the resulting geometry encodes a calibrated probability axis. We further test cross-validation against two independent psychometric datasets \citep{vogel2022systematic,wintle2019verbal}, zero-shot ranking transfer to eight typologically diverse languages, robustness to dimensional truncation, null-hypothesis controls, and \textbf{concept erasure as functional validation} --- the embedding-class analogue of the causal-intervention experiments standard in the decoder-LLM linear-feature literature.

\textbf{Our contributions:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{A calibrated within-type verbal probability axis triangulated across three psychometric datasets.} Five architecturally diverse embedding models recover a single linear direction within syntactic types (Spearman \(\rho > 0.90\) supervised, 0.59--0.94 leave-one-out on the 53-expression \citet{mosteller1990quantifying} dataset). The axis cross-validates against two independent psychometric datasets spanning over fifty years of replication: Mosteller\(\to\)\citet{vogel2022systematic} \(\rho = 0.991\), Mosteller\(\to\)\citet{wintle2019verbal} \(\rho = 0.967\) (\(n \approx 924\)). Convergence across datasets collected by independent groups on different populations argues against an artifact of any single calibration source. To our knowledge this is the first demonstration of such structure in frozen pretrained pooled sentence embeddings.
\item
  \textbf{An embedding-class structural analogue of decoder-LLM causal intervention.} Rank-1 representation-level concept erasure of the probability axis from cross-type embeddings raises calibration MAE by 17--25 percentage points on the predicative\(\leftrightarrow\)modal pair, with the headline pair clearing two complementary nulls --- a cosine-matched random-direction control (testing geometric correlation) and a label-permutation null on the eraser axis's training labels (testing probability content) --- at \(p = 0.002\) in all four model \(\times\) direction combinations across two architectures. Cross-pair Pearson \(r(\cos, \Delta\mathrm{MAE}) = 0.92 / 0.86\) across all twelve ordered cross-type pairs is the structural signature confirming that downstream linear decoders use the probability content the axis carries, not merely correlated embedding geometry.
\item
  \textbf{Cross-architecture and cross-linguistic robustness, with informative negatives.} The finding holds across six pretrained embedding models spanning five architectural families (BERT, BERT-large, MoE, decoder-derived embedding heads, multilingual XLM-R-based) and ranks hedge expressions zero-shot in eight typologically diverse languages via a multilingual encoder (mean ranking \(|\rho| = 0.93\)). Permutation null tests on the three larger-\(n\) syntactic types yield \(p \leq 0.005\), and a grammatically clean evaluative non-epistemic control returns LOO \(\rho = -0.41\) versus 0.87 for real hedges. Three negative results sharpen the picture: interpretive precision (Mosteller IQR width) is not in the embedding geometry; no ensemble of within-type axes beats the single modal axis on novel-phrase generalization; and negation breaks linear composition in the geometrically appropriate manner of a probability-reflecting operation.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}\label{related-work}

Three lines of recent work motivate, but do not subsume, the question we ask. The first establishes that pretrained language models encode many human-meaningful concepts as linear directions, but does so almost entirely on decoder LLM internal states with token-level causal intervention as the validation method. The second establishes that verbal-probability semantics are recoverable from large language models, but elicits them behaviorally through prompting rather than geometrically from representations. The third establishes that pooled sentence representations carry graded epistemic content, but for cloze probability, NLI inference strength, or rhetorical certainty rather than for the verbal-probability hedge lexicon, and not as a frozen, psychometrically calibrated linear axis. We position our contribution at the intersection these three lines leave open, and close §2 with an explicit gap statement.

\subsection{Linear features in decoder LLM internal states}\label{linear-features-in-decoder-llm-internal-states}

The Linear Representation Hypothesis --- that human-meaningful concepts correspond to linear directions in language model representations --- has been formalized and tested most extensively on decoder LLM internal states \citep{park2024linear}. \citet{marks2023geometry} identify a single ``truth direction'' in residual stream activations that separates true from false factual statements; \citet{burger2024truth} refine this representation to handle a polarity confound; \citet{yu2025directions} generalize one-dimensional truth directions into multi-dimensional cones for propositional facts. Within this lineage, \citet{ji2025calibrating} is the most direct framing-level comparator to the present work. They identify a single ``Verbal Uncertainty Feature'' (VUF) in the residual streams of Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen-2.5-7B by computing a difference-in-means direction over question--answer pairs labeled high- versus low-verbal-uncertainty by an LLM-as-a-Judge protocol, and they validate the feature causally by steering activations along it at inference time to produce more or less hedged generations and reduce overconfident hallucinations. \citet{lepori2026fantasy} extract ``modal difference vectors'' from late-layer hidden states of GPT-2, Llama-3.2, OLMo-2, and Gemma-2 models that linearly discriminate four scenario-level modal categories --- \emph{probable}, \emph{improbable}, \emph{impossible}, \emph{inconceivable} --- across six expert-labeled datasets, demonstrate that projection magnitudes onto these vectors track fine-grained human categorization behavior, and provide preliminary causal-steering evidence that the directions are not epiphenomenal. \citet{valois2025frame} extend the LRH from single tokens to multi-token ``frames'' living on the unembedding matrix and demonstrate functional content via Top-\emph{k} Concept-Guided Decoding. All four of these works share two methodological commitments: they operate on \textbf{decoder LLM internal activations} --- residual streams, late-layer hidden states, unembedding matrices --- and they validate functional content via \textbf{token-level causal intervention} (steering, activation patching, guided decoding), naturally available because the model generates tokens. The lines of evidence they assemble are complementary to ours within the LRH frame; the model class, the available intervention method, and (for Ji and Lepori) the calibration target differ from what we study, in ways §2.5 makes explicit.

\subsection{Verbal-probability semantics elicited behaviorally from language models}\label{verbal-probability-semantics-elicited-behaviorally-from-language-models}

A parallel literature investigates how language models interpret verbal probability expressions like ``likely,'' ``probably,'' and ``highly unlikely'' by \textbf{prompting} the model and comparing its numerical outputs to human survey baselines. \citet{sileo2023probing} probe pretrained models for words-of-estimative-probability classification using fine-tuned, task-specific objectives. \citet{belem2024perceptions} compare ten LLMs against 94 human participants on 14 uncertainty expressions drawn from \citet{wallsten1986measuring} and \citet{wallsten2008communicating}, framing the task as theory-of-mind (``Sonia believes it is unlikely it will rain today'' --- quantify Sonia's certainty, not your own) and finding that 7 of 10 LLMs map uncertainty to probabilities in human-aligned ways but are substantially more biased by prior knowledge than humans are. \citet{tang2026evaluation} evaluate 17 Words of Estimative Probability across GPT-3.5, GPT-4, two Llama-2 variants, and ERNIE-4 against a human survey baseline, finding human--LLM alignment for high-certainty expressions but divergence on the majority of mid-range expressions and additional divergence under gendered-role and Chinese-language prompting. \citet{wang2024calibrating} calibrate certainty-phrase distributions against human data using transport-based methods at the phrase level, again without embedding analysis. These works collectively establish that verbal probability semantics are quantitatively recoverable from contemporary LLMs and that human population-level probability mappings for hedge expressions are robust enough to serve as a comparison standard. They locate the phenomenon \textbf{behaviorally}, in model outputs, rather than geometrically, in model representations.

\subsection{Probing pretrained sentence representations for human-aligned graded properties}\label{probing-pretrained-sentence-representations-for-human-aligned-graded-properties}

A third, smaller line studies pooled or encoded sentence representations directly. The strongest precursor in our model class is \citet{jacobs2022masked}: mean-pooled RoBERTa sentence embeddings, with the critical final word replaced by \texttt{\textless{}mask\textgreater{}}, are passed through 282 leave-one-out regularized logistic-regression classifiers trained to discriminate strong- versus weak-sentential-constraint sentences from the \citet{federmeier2007multifaceted} stimulus set; the classifier's predicted probability is then correlated against the cloze probability of the masked critical word (\(\hat\rho = 0.43\)) and against the cloze entropy of human responses (\(\hat\rho = -0.32\)). The differentiation runs two layers deep. \emph{Phenomenon:} their target is sentential constraint operationalized through next-word predictability --- uncertainty about which word will come next given a preceding context --- whereas our target is the verbal-probability semantics of explicit hedge expressions (``probably'' → 71\%, ``possible'' → 39\%) collected from human raters. \emph{Method:} they train per-item binary classifiers and then correlate classifier output with a continuous human signal external to the classifier; we directly regress pooled sentence embedding differences onto continuous psychometric medians, extracting a single linear axis whose calibration is the geometric object of study. They do not extract a calibrated verbal-probability axis, do not cross-validate against independent psychometric datasets, and do not test cross-linguistic transfer. \citet{chen2019uncertain} refine NLI annotation from categorical labels to continuous subjective probability via the u-SNLI dataset (61,597 MTurk-elicited probability annotations on premise--hypothesis pairs), then fine-tune scalar regression models from BERT-derived sentence representations; the phenomenon is sentence-pair entailment probability, the method is fine-tuned scalar regression rather than frozen-geometry probing, and no general probability axis is identified. \citet{schuster2019harnessing} predict human scalar pragmatic ratings (scalar implicature strength) from task-trained sentence encoders. \citet{pei2021measuring} regress continuous certainty in scientific writing from fine-tuned transformer encoders, locating rhetorical certainty rather than verbal-probability semantics. \citet{lee2015event} and \citet{stanovsky2017integrating} predict scalar factuality with structured task-specific models. \citet{bhatia2017vector} shows distributional vector-space models predict subjective probability judgments for real-world events from keyword associations, predating sentence-embedding architectures. \citet{shen2023sen2pro} layer model and data uncertainty over pretrained sentence encoders, modeling distributional embedding noise rather than human psychometric semantics. Together, these works establish that pooled sentence representations carry \emph{some} graded epistemic content --- but for cloze probability, NLI inference strength, scalar implicature, rhetorical certainty, factuality, or generic event likelihood, and not as a frozen, psychometrically calibrated verbal-probability axis cross-validated against independent psychometric datasets.

\subsection{Verbal-probability psychometrics as ground truth}\label{verbal-probability-psychometrics-as-ground-truth}

The data side of this paper draws on a sixty-year tradition of verbal-probability calibration studies. \citet{lichtenstein1967empirical} and \citet{beythmarom1982people} established that population-level mappings from verbal expressions to numerical probabilities are systematic and reproducible. \citet{wallsten1986measuring}, \citet{wallsten2008communicating}, and \citet{budescu1995processing} developed the methodological framework --- non-verifiable contexts, careful statement construction, distributional rather than point estimates --- that the modern literature continues to use. \citet{mosteller1990quantifying} provide the primary calibration corpus we train on: 53 verbal probability expressions rated by 238 science writers, with median, P25, P75, and IQR per expression. \citet{vogel2022systematic} is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 such studies spanning 1967--2018, which we use as an independent cross-validation target. \citet{wintle2019verbal} (\(n \approx 924\)) is a third independent dataset, collected on a different population with a different protocol, providing an additional cross-validation target. \citet{lassiter2017graded} develops the formal-semantics theory of graded modality --- degree-based rather than possible-worlds --- that motivates treating ``probably,'' ``possibly,'' and their kin as continuous-valued operators in the first place. \citet{schockaert2022formal} provides a formal framework for embeddings as epistemic states, supplying the measurement-theoretic scaffolding for the convergent-measurement perspective we adopt in §5.

\subsection{The gap}\label{the-gap}

Across these three lines, no prior work demonstrates the conjunction this paper fills:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Continuously calibrated} rather than categorically classified. \citet{sileo2023probing} classify; \citet{jacobs2022masked} train binary classifiers and correlate their outputs with continuous external signals; we regress pooled embedding differences directly onto psychometric medians, on the same percentage scale humans use.
\item
  \textbf{Verbal probability} specifically --- the hedge lexicon (``likely,'' ``probably,'' ``doubtful,'' ``almost certain'') --- rather than truth, factuality, sentential constraint, NLI inference probability, modal categorization of event plausibility, or scalar implicature strength.
\item
  \textbf{Frozen pretrained pooled sentence embeddings}, rather than decoder LLM internal activations \citep{ji2025calibrating,lepori2026fantasy,marks2023geometry,yu2025directions,valois2025frame} or fine-tuned task-specific models \citep{sileo2023probing,chen2019uncertain,pei2021measuring}.
\item
  \textbf{Aligned with human psychometric judgments} \citep{mosteller1990quantifying,wallsten1986measuring} rather than with model-internal LLM-as-a-Judge labels \citep{ji2025calibrating} or expert-assigned modal-category labels \citep{lepori2026fantasy}.
\item
  \textbf{Validated against independent psychometric datasets} \citep{vogel2022systematic,wintle2019verbal}, spanning over fifty years of replication, rather than against a single calibration source.
\end{enumerate}

Each qualifier on its own excludes a class of near-misses; together they identify the open territory this paper occupies. The contribution is parallel in spirit to the decoder-LLM linear-feature literature --- same family of finding, namely that a graded epistemic property is recoverable as a linear direction in a pretrained representation --- but is conducted in a model class where token-level causal intervention is not available, where representation-level concept erasure (§4.4) is the appropriate analogue, and where human psychometric data, rather than model behavior, is the appropriate calibration target.

\section{Method}\label{method}

We extract a verbal probability axis from frozen pretrained pooled sentence embeddings, calibrate it against human psychometric medians, and evaluate it against in-sample fit, leave-one-out generalization, two independent psychometric datasets, eight typologically diverse languages, several baselines, three null-hypothesis controls, and a representation-level concept-erasure protocol. The protocol is identical across experiments: every script in the codebase is self-contained and reuses the same difference-vector construction, ridge-regression objective, and linear calibration step, parameterized only by the syntactic type of the hedge expressions and the embedding model. Math notation: vectors are column vectors, \(\|\cdot\|\) is the \(\ell_2\) norm, \(\hat{v} = v/\|v\|\) denotes the unit-normalized form of \(v\), \(\rho\) is Spearman rank correlation, and MAE is mean absolute error in percentage points.

\subsection{Data}\label{data}

\textbf{Primary calibration: \citet{mosteller1990quantifying}.} We use the full 53-expression \citet{mosteller1990quantifying} corpus as the primary calibration set (\(n = 238\) science writers, with 25th-percentile, median, 75th-percentile, and inter-quartile-range probability values per expression on a \([0, 100]\) scale). The dataset is provided in \texttt{docs/mosteller\_youtz\_1990\_full.csv}. We use the median as the target probability throughout; the IQR is reserved for the precision-encoding probe in §4.7.

\textbf{Cross-validation datasets.} Two independent psychometric datasets test whether the trained axis generalizes beyond the calibration source. \citet{vogel2022systematic} is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 verbal-probability studies spanning 1967--2018, supplied as \texttt{docs/vogel\_2022\_systematic\_review.csv}; we extract the median pooled across studies for each expression that matches our syntactic types. \citet{wintle2019verbal} (\(n \approx 924\)) provides a third independent dataset; we transcribe nine predicative and three frequency-adverbial values from their Figure 2 and Table 1 (hardcoded in \texttt{experiment\_08\_bimodality\_wintle.py}). All three sources collect aggregate human probability judgments under non-verifiable contexts following the methodological framework of \citet{wallsten1986measuring} and \citet{budescu1995processing}; the convergence of three datasets collected by different groups in different decades on different populations is the basis for the cross-dataset generalization claim in §4.2.

\textbf{Type classification.} Mixing syntactic types confounds the analysis: PCA on the 52 mixed-type Mosteller difference vectors recovers PC1 as a syntactic-frame direction (28.7\% of variance, ordering noun-phrase constructions against frequency adverbs) rather than as the probability axis (FINDINGS-01). Within-type analysis is therefore not a methodological convenience but a load-bearing decision that isolates the semantic signal from the syntactic envelope (§4.1; cf.~the polarity confound \citealp{burger2024truth} report for truth directions). We partition the Mosteller expressions into four syntactic types, each with a single sentence template that holds syntax constant across all expressions of that type. Let \(T_{\text{type}}(x)\) denote the template for syntactic type with hedge expression \(x\) substituted for the placeholder, and let \(s_0\) denote the bare claim ``The experiment will succeed.'' The four types and their templates are:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Predicative adjective} (\(n = 13\)): \$T\_\{\text{pred}\}(x) = \$ ``It is \(x\) that the experiment will succeed.''
\item
  \textbf{Frequency adverb} (\(n = 19\)): \$T\_\{\text{freq}\}(x) = \$ ``The experiment will \(x\) succeed.''
\item
  \textbf{Noun phrase} (\(n = 11\)): \$T\_\{\text{np}\}(x) = \$ ``There is a(n) \(x\) that the experiment will succeed.''
\item
  \textbf{Modal adverb} (\(n = 10\)): \$T\_\{\text{mod}\}(x) = \$ ``The experiment will \(x\) succeed.''
\end{itemize}

The frequency-adverb and modal-adverb templates share a syntactic slot but encode different semantic types (base-rate frequency versus epistemic confidence); the modal axis is not derivable from the frequency axis (§4.1, FINDINGS-03). Modal training is restricted to the ten expressions with Mosteller-grounded probabilities --- adverbial forms of Mosteller predicative adjectives such as \texttt{certainly}, \texttt{probably}, and \texttt{possibly} --- to keep the calibration target purely psychometric. The seven additional modal adverbs used in early exploratory work (\texttt{perhaps}, \texttt{conceivably}, \texttt{arguably}, etc.) carry author-estimated probabilities and are excluded from the load-bearing axis training; they reappear as held-out novel phrases in §4.5.

\subsection{Models}\label{models}

We test six pretrained embedding models, accessed through the Ollama embedding endpoint at \texttt{http://localhost:11434/api/embed}. Five models are used for the within-type analyses; the sixth (bge-m3) supports the multilingual experiment. We make no fine-tuning, no head training, and no architectural modifications; the qualifier ``frozen pretrained'' in the novelty claim depends on this.

The five within-type models span five distinct architectural families (BERT, BERT-large, Mixture of Experts, decoder-derived heads, and Qwen3) and three training paradigms; bge-m3 adds a multilingual XLM-R-based encoder trained on more than one hundred languages. All five within-type models output a single mean- or {[}CLS{]}-pooled sentence vector per input. Cross-architecture robustness (§4.1) is the basis for the claim that the verbal probability axis is a property of pretrained pooled-embedding geometry rather than of any specific architecture or training corpus.

\subsection{Axis extraction}\label{axis-extraction}

\textbf{Difference-vector construction.} For each syntactic type \(T\) with expressions \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}\) and Mosteller medians \(\{y_1, \ldots, y_n\}\), we embed the bare claim \(s_0\) and each templated sentence \(T(x_i)\) using the model's pooled output, yielding \(\mathbf{e}_0\) and \(\{\mathbf{e}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n\}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). The input feature for expression \(x_i\) is the difference vector
\[
\mathbf{d}_i \;=\; \mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{e}_0,
\]
which subtracts off the propositional content shared across all expressions in the type and isolates the contribution of the hedge phrase. Differencing against a shared bare claim is the same construction \citet{mikolov2013linguistic} used to expose word-level analogies and that the decoder-LLM linear-feature literature uses to extract truth and uncertainty directions from residual streams \citep{marks2023geometry,ji2025calibrating}.

\textbf{Ridge regression on Mosteller medians.} We standardize the medians \(\tilde{y}_i = (y_i - \bar{y})/\mathrm{std}(y)\) and stack the difference vectors as rows of \(D \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\). The probability axis is the unit-normalized solution to a ridge regression \citep{hoerl1970ridge} with regularization \(\lambda = 0.1\):
\[
\mathbf{w}^{*} \;=\; \bigl(D^{\top} D + \lambda I_d\bigr)^{-1} D^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{y}}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{w}} \;=\; \mathbf{w}^{*} / \|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|.
\]
Solving the linear system in \(d\) dimensions on \(n \le 19\) samples is severely under-determined; the ridge term selects the minimum-norm solution along the dominant probability-correlated direction in the column span of \(D\) and stabilizes against numerical conditioning issues at the high embedding dimensions (\(d \in \{768, 1024, 4096\}\)). The choice \(\lambda = 0.1\) is fixed across all experiments and all models for cross-cell comparability rather than per-cell optimum: a four-decade sweep on \(\lambda \in \{0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10\}\) across nomic-embed-text v1.5 and mxbai-embed-large by all four within-type axes (eight cells) confirms that LOO Spearman \(\rho\) remains within 0.072 of the \(\lambda = 0.1\) reference everywhere, with the worst-case drop on nomic predicative (\(\rho = 0.874\) at \(\lambda = 0.1\) falling to \(0.802\) at \(\lambda = 10\)). The sweep is asymmetric, however: on six of the eight (model \(\times\) type) cells a smaller \(\lambda\) would yield a higher LOO \(\rho\) than \(\lambda = 0.1\), and the modal axis is the cell where regularizer choice does the most rank shuffling --- most strikingly mxbai modal, where the reference \(\lambda = 0.1\) sits at the sweep minimum (LOO \(\rho = 0.806\), vs.~\(0.903\) at \(\lambda = 0.001\) and \(0.869\) at \(\lambda = 10\)), consistent with the small-\(n\) rank-saturation regime developed in §6 (L7).

\textbf{Linear calibration.} The unit axis \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}\) ranks expressions correctly but does not return probabilities on the percentage scale humans use. We recover the calibration via ordinary least squares on the in-sample projections \(p_i = \mathbf{d}_i^{\top} \hat{\mathbf{w}}\) against the unstandardized Mosteller medians \(y_i\):
\[
\hat{y}_i \;=\; \alpha \cdot \mathbf{d}_i^{\top} \hat{\mathbf{w}} + \beta, \qquad \text{with } (\alpha, \beta) \text{ from } \mathrm{OLS}\bigl(\{p_i\}, \{y_i\}\bigr).
\]
Predicted probabilities are clipped to \([0, 100]\). The calibration is a one-dimensional affine map; it cannot improve ranking over the unit projection but is what allows continuous predictions on the same percentage scale used in psychometric reporting, and is what the abstract's ``continuously calibrated'' qualifier refers to. We train one \((\hat{\mathbf{w}}, \alpha, \beta)\) triple per (model, syntactic type) pair, yielding twenty axes for the within-type analyses (five models × four types) plus the eight cross-linguistic axes (bge-m3 × eight languages × \{predicative, modal\}). Sentence templates use a single propositional content (``the experiment will succeed'') for the load-bearing analyses; FINDINGS-01 reports cross-content validation showing axis ranking \(\rho > 0.69\) on alternative bare claims (``the treatment will be effective'', ``the prediction will be correct'').

\subsection{Evaluation}\label{evaluation}

Five evaluation strands address generalization, baselines, null hypotheses, cross-linguistic transfer, and functional content respectively. All Spearman correlations and MAE values are computed against held-out targets except the in-sample diagnostics explicitly labeled as such.

\textbf{In-sample fit and leave-one-out generalization.} For each (model, type) we report in-sample Spearman \(\rho\) between calibrated predictions and Mosteller medians, and leave-one-out (LOO) Spearman \(\rho\) obtained by retraining \((\hat{\mathbf{w}}, \alpha, \beta)\) on the \(n-1\) remaining expressions, predicting the held-out one, and correlating the \(n\) LOO predictions against the medians. We complement LOO \(\rho\) with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals over 10,000 resamples of the (prediction, median) pairs (\texttt{paper\_validation.py:spearman\_ci\_bootstrap}, fixed seed 42). For psychometric ground truths with \(n = 10\)--\(19\) per type, the LOO--bootstrap pairing is the appropriate generalization summary; the small \(n\) regime saturates rank-based metrics when in-sample \(\rho \geq 0.95\), a methodological constraint we return to in the concept-erasure analysis (§4.4) and limitations (§6).

\textbf{Cross-dataset evaluation.} The Mosteller-trained axis is applied without retraining to two independent psychometric datasets. For \citet{vogel2022systematic}, expressions are matched by surface form and embedded in the same syntactic templates as the Mosteller training data; predicted probabilities are compared against Vogel medians via Spearman \(\rho\) and MAE. The \citet{wintle2019verbal} protocol is identical, applied separately to predicative and frequency-adverbial expressions. No expression overlap between training and test is filtered: we treat the two datasets as offering the same population-level mapping refined on different samples, and Mosteller→Vogel and Mosteller→Wintle correlations as the appropriate measure of population-level recovery rather than as out-of-sample novelty tests. Novel-phrase generalization beyond the psychometric corpora is handled separately in §4.5 using author-rated targets.

\textbf{Baselines.} For each syntactic type we report three unsupervised baselines alongside the supervised ridge axis, all using the same calibration step (3.3) for fair comparison:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Random direction.} A unit vector drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\) and normalized; we report mean and standard deviation across 100 independent samples (\texttt{paper\_validation.py:run\_baselines}, fixed seed 42).
\item
  \textbf{Mean-difference direction.} \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{mean}} = \widehat{\overline{\mathbf{d}}}\) where \(\overline{\mathbf{d}}\) is the centroid of the difference vectors. This is the unsupervised counterpart of the ridge axis and the construction used by \citet{marks2023geometry} and \citet{ji2025calibrating} for difference-in-means truth and uncertainty features.
\item
  \textbf{PCA PC1.} The first principal component of the centered difference matrix, capturing the dominant direction of variation regardless of probability ground truth.
\end{enumerate}

The baseline comparison addresses whether the supervised signal is genuinely probability-aligned: a random direction with the same calibration step bounds the floor; PC1 indicates how much of the probability signal is recoverable without supervision; the mean-difference direction tests whether a single ``hedge insertion'' centroid suffices in the absence of probability labels.

\textbf{Null hypothesis controls.} Three controls (\texttt{experiment\_10\_null\_hypothesis.py}) test whether the observed effect could arise from the protocol independently of the hedge semantics: (i) a permutation test that shuffles Mosteller medians among the expressions and re-runs LOO 1\{,\}000 times, reporting the empirical \(p\)-value of the observed real-label \(\rho\); (ii) a non-epistemic adjective control that substitutes adjectives without epistemic content (e.g., scenic, metallic) into the same predicative template and trains a putative ``axis'' against author-assigned arbitrary ratings; (iii) a random-label control that draws Uniform\((0, 100)\) values per expression, runs the full ridge-plus-LOO pipeline, and tabulates how often the random-label LOO \(\rho\) exceeds the real-label LOO \(\rho\) across 1\{,\}000 trials. Results in §4.6.

\textbf{Cross-linguistic protocol.} Using bge-m3 (1024d, XLM-R, multilingual; \citealp{chen2024bge}), we train predicative and modal axes on English Mosteller data following §3.3, then apply each axis without retraining to translated hedge expressions in eight typologically diverse languages: German, French, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, and Hindi. Each language uses a translated bare claim and translated syntactic templates analogous to the English ones; difference vectors are computed against the language-matched bare claim before projection onto the English-trained axis. The primary metric is Spearman \(\rho\) between ranked projections and the English Mosteller equivalents of each translated expression --- a \emph{ranking} transfer claim that does not depend on the translation preserving exact numerical calibration. We report MAE as a secondary diagnostic. The conditions under which native-speaker calibration would be required for a valid MAE comparison, and the resulting limits on what transfers and what does not, are discussed in §6 (L2). Implementation: \texttt{experiment\_09\_cross\_linguistic.py}.

\textbf{Concept erasure.} As the embedding-class analogue of the causal-intervention protocols standard in the decoder-LLM linear-feature literature \citep{ji2025calibrating,marks2023geometry,valois2025frame}, we test whether the probability axis is functional rather than merely correlated by erasing it from one syntactic type's embeddings via rank-1 projection and measuring degradation of probability prediction along a different type's axis. For ordered pair \((A, B)\) with \(A, B \in \{\text{predicative}, \text{frequency}, \text{noun phrase}, \text{modal}\}\) and \(A \neq B\), we erase the type-\(A\) axis \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_A\) from each type-\(B\) difference vector via the rank-1 projection
\[
\mathbf{d}_i' \;=\; \mathbf{d}_i - (\mathbf{d}_i^{\top} \hat{\mathbf{w}}_A)\, \hat{\mathbf{w}}_A,
\]
then re-decode with type \(B\)'s calibrated triple \((\hat{\mathbf{w}}_B, \alpha_B, \beta_B)\) and compare in-sample \(\rho\) and MAE before and after erasure. Geometric overlap alone --- erasing any direction with non-trivial \(\cos(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_A, \hat{\mathbf{w}}_B)\) --- would degrade prediction; the relevant question is whether erasing the \emph{probability} axis degrades prediction \emph{more} than erasing a direction with the same overlap. We therefore compare against a cosine-matched random control: 100 unit directions \(\mathbf{r}\) constructed so that \(|\cos(\mathbf{r}, \hat{\mathbf{w}}_B)| = |\cos(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_A, \hat{\mathbf{w}}_B)|\) by sampling \(\mathbf{r} = \pm c\,\hat{\mathbf{w}}_B + \sqrt{1 - c^2}\,\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\perp}\) with \(c = |\cos(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_A, \hat{\mathbf{w}}_B)|\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\perp}\) a random unit vector orthogonal to \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_B\). The two-part design --- real-axis rank-1 erasure plus cosine-matched random null --- is what isolates \emph{functional} probability content from geometric overlap. Full results, the choice of MAE versus \(\rho\) as the load-bearing metric under small-\(n\) rank-saturation, and the cross-pair \(\Delta\mathrm{MAE}\) versus inter-axis cosine signature are presented in §4.4. Implementation: \texttt{experiment\_11\_concept\_erasure.py}, run on mxbai-embed-large (1024d) and qwen3-embedding (4096d) for cross-architecture robustness.

\section{Results}\label{results}

\subsection{The syntactic confound and within-type probability axes}\label{the-syntactic-confound-and-within-type-probability-axes}

When verbal probability expressions are pooled across the four syntactic types of §3.1, the dominant linear direction in the embedding space is \emph{not} probability but syntax. PCA on the 52 mixed-type difference vectors \(\{\mathbf{d}_i\}\) from nomic-embed-text v1.5 returns a first principal component that explains 28.7\% of the variance, and inspection of its extremes orders constructions by template family rather than by Mosteller median: noun-phrase formulations such as ``high probability,'' ``very high probability,'' and ``moderate probability'' sit at one end, frequency adverbs such as ``very infrequent,'' ``not often,'' and ``not very often'' at the other. The probability signal appears only on PC2 (14.8\% of variance, \(\rho = -0.68\) against the medians, \(p = 2.4 \times 10^{-8}\)), and PC1 itself correlates only weakly with the medians (\(\rho = -0.28\), \(p = 0.05\)). The \emph{largest} axis of variation in the cross-type difference-vector cloud is therefore a syntactic-frame direction onto which probability projects only as a secondary signal. This is the structural counterpart in pretrained pooled sentence embeddings of the polarity confound \citet{burger2024truth} report for truth directions in decoder LLM residual streams: a candidate semantic direction recovered without controlling for a co-varying syntactic property is contaminated by that property.

Holding the syntactic type fixed reverses this picture. Within each of the four type partitions, a single ridge-regression axis \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}\) trained on Mosteller medians by the protocol of §3.3 recovers the probability ordering with high in-sample fidelity and generalizes through leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation. Table 1 reports both metrics across the five within-type embedding models. In-sample Spearman \(\rho\) exceeds 0.90 for every (model, type) cell --- the supervised claim foregrounded in the abstract --- and LOO \(\rho\) falls in the range 0.59--0.94, with embeddinggemma's predicative axis reaching the highest in-sample fit (0.99) and nomic-embed-text v1.5's noun-phrase axis reaching the highest LOO (\(\rho = 0.94\)). The two LOO cells below 0.65 (embeddinggemma modal at 0.59 and nomic-embed-text v1.5 modal at 0.65) are the small-sample saturation regime \(\rho\)-based metrics enter at \(n = 10\) training items; we discuss this and its implications for the §4.4 concept-erasure analysis in §6 (L7). The dominance of probability on the within-type difference-vector cloud is also visible without supervision: PCA PC1 within type reaches \(\rho = 0.98\) against the Mosteller medians on noun phrases for nomic-embed-text v1.5 (PC1 explains 36\% of the within-type variance), \(\rho = 0.93\) for predicative on mxbai-embed-large (PC1 = 60\%), and \(\rho = 0.96\) for noun phrase on qwen3-embedding (PC1 = 61\%). The abstract's ``Spearman \(\rho > 0.90\) supervised, 0.59--0.94 LOO'' claim refers to Table 1.

The same finding holds across five architectural families --- BERT (nomic v1.5), BERT-large (mxbai), Mixture-of-Experts (nomic v2 MoE), decoder-derived embedding heads (embeddinggemma, qwen3) --- and three training paradigms. \subsection{Three-dataset psychometric triangulation}\label{three-dataset-psychometric-triangulation}

The \citet{mosteller1990quantifying} calibration is sixty years old and has been replicated repeatedly under different protocols and on different populations. We test whether the within-type axes trained on Mosteller medians transfer, \emph{without retraining}, to two independently collected psychometric corpora: the \citet{vogel2022systematic} systematic review and meta-analysis aggregating 21 verbal-probability studies from 1967 to 2018, and the \citet{wintle2019verbal} experiment (\(n \approx 924\)) drawing on a different population with a different elicitation protocol. The Mosteller-trained axis \((\hat{\mathbf{w}}, \alpha, \beta)\) is applied as in §3.4 to surface-form-matched expressions embedded in the same syntactic templates; we report Spearman \(\rho\) and MAE on the Vogel and Wintle medians.

For predicative expressions --- the type with the largest cross-corpus overlap (\(n_{\text{test}} = 11\) for Vogel, 9 for Wintle) --- Mosteller-to-Vogel correlations exceed 0.89 across all five models and reach 0.991 on mxbai-embed-large with MAE = 5.1 percentage points (Table 2). Mosteller-to-Wintle predicative results are comparable: \(\rho = 0.967\) on mxbai-embed-large (MAE = 3.6\%) and \(\rho \geq 0.917\) on nomic-embed-text v1.5 and qwen3-embedding (MAE between 3.5\% and 6.9\%). The frequency-adverb cross-validation is more limited by overlap (\(n_{\text{test}} = 3\) on both Vogel and Wintle), but Vogel returns \(\rho = 1.000\) on three of the five models with MAEs between 2.4\% and 6.7\%, and Wintle returns \(\rho = 1.000\) on every tested model with MAEs of 4.0--10.5\%. Noun-phrase expressions have no cross-corpus matches and are not included in the table; the cross-corpus tests therefore probe predicative and frequency-adverbial calibration directly.

Three observations follow. First, the strongest single predicative cross-dataset result --- mxbai-embed-large's \(\rho = 0.991\) against Vogel --- is essentially indistinguishable from the in-sample Mosteller fit (0.967, Table 1) for the same model and type, indicating that the axis recovers a population-level mapping rather than overfitting Mosteller's specific 1990 sample. Second, the convergence is independent of architecture: BERT-base, BERT-large, MoE, and decoder-derived embedding heads all clear \(\rho \geq 0.89\) on Mosteller-to-Vogel predicative. Third, Wintle's calibration is recovered with MAE as low as 3.5\% (qwen3-embedding) and 3.6\% (mxbai-embed-large), tighter than the in-sample Mosteller LOO MAE on the same models, a pattern consistent with Wintle's larger participant pool (\(n \approx 924\) versus Mosteller's 238) producing tighter population medians than Mosteller's, against which the same axis happens to align as well or better. Figure 2 plots the headline single-figure cross-validation against Vogel; Figure 3 places Mosteller, Vogel, and Wintle predicative medians on the same axis, showing the three datasets fall on a common line modulo independent sampling noise.

This is the empirical content of the abstract's claim that the verbal probability axis cross-validates against ``convergence of three independent psychometric datasets spanning over fifty years of replication.'' The three sources were collected by different research groups in different decades on different populations using different elicitation protocols; their joint agreement with the embedding-derived axis argues against any artifact of a single calibration corpus.

\subsection{Cross-linguistic ranking transfer}\label{cross-linguistic-ranking-transfer}

We test whether the verbal probability axis is a property of English specifically or of multilingual pretrained representations more generally. Using bge-m3 (1024d, XLM-RoBERTa-based, trained on 100+ languages; \citealp{chen2024bge}), we train predicative and modal axes on the English Mosteller corpus following §3.3 and then apply each axis, \emph{without retraining}, to translated hedge expressions in eight typologically diverse languages: German, French, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, and Hindi. The expected probability of each translated expression is taken to be the Mosteller median of its English equivalent --- a translation pairing rather than a native-speaker psychometric value, with the consequences discussed below and treated formally in §6 L2. The primary metric is therefore Spearman \(\rho\), a \emph{ranking} claim that does not depend on the translation preserving exact numerical calibration; MAE is reported as a secondary diagnostic.

\textbf{Table 3.} Zero-shot ranking transfer of the English-trained bge-m3 axis to eight typologically diverse languages. Predicative axis cos compares the English-trained axis to a per-language axis trained on translated Mosteller equivalents (§3.3 protocol applied per language). Mean \(|\rho|\) across all 16 (language, frame) cells = 0.928. Source: \texttt{results/exp09\_bge-m3\_8lang.txt}.

Sixteen of sixteen (language, frame) combinations clear \(\rho \geq 0.83\), with mean \(|\rho| = 0.928\). Korean predicative reaches \(\rho = 1.000\) on \(n = 8\), Hindi modal reaches \(\rho = 1.000\) on \(n = 6\), and Chinese modal reaches \(\rho = 0.991\) on \(n = 7\) --- three results from typologically distant Indo-European, Indo-Aryan, and Sino-Tibetan branches. Per-language axis-alignment cosines, computed by training a separate ridge axis on each language's translated Mosteller expressions and measuring its cosine with the English-trained axis, are above 0.75 for every predicative axis tested and cluster at 0.94 for German, French, and Spanish (the typologically closest to English) and at 0.85--0.87 for Korean, Japanese, Arabic, and Hindi. Japanese and Korean are the only language pair whose predicative axes align more strongly with each other (cos = 0.900) than with English (0.845, 0.865), consistent with their parallel epistemic-marker morphology. Figure 4 shows the per-language predicative-axis projection ordering.

The MAE column tells a more nuanced story than the \(\rho\) column. Arabic modal MAE reaches 3.6\% --- comparable to Wintle's 3.6\% (Table 2). Japanese modal MAE, by contrast, is 18.1\%, driven by single expressions whose translation pairing is a known approximation: pragmatic-loaded Japanese epistemic markers carry contextual implicatures the template-based evaluation cannot capture, and the ``expected'' probability column is itself a translation-pairing artifact rather than a native-speaker calibration. The Japanese modal MAE is therefore not a calibration failure of the axis --- the ranking remains \(\rho = 0.857\) --- but a translation-pairing artifact that exposes the limit of the present cross-linguistic protocol. We treat ranking transfer as the load-bearing claim and calibration MAE as a secondary, preliminary diagnostic that requires native-speaker psychometric replication in each target language to interpret rigorously; §6 L2 develops this position in full.

\subsection{Functional validation via concept erasure}\label{functional-validation-via-concept-erasure}

The §3.4 protocol --- rank-1 erasure of axis \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_A\) from type-\(B\) difference vectors followed by re-decoding with type \(B\)'s calibrated triple --- applied across all twelve ordered pairs \((A, B)\) with \(A \neq B\) and \(A, B \in \{\text{predicative}, \text{frequency adverb}, \text{noun phrase}, \text{modal}\}\) on mxbai-embed-large (1024d) and qwen3-embedding (4096d), yields a single cross-model structural signature. The Pearson correlation between inter-axis cosine alignment \(\cos(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_A, \hat{\mathbf{w}}_B)\) and the increase in calibrated mean absolute prediction error after erasure (\(\Delta\mathrm{MAE}\)) is \(r = 0.92\) on mxbai-embed-large and \(r = 0.86\) on qwen3-embedding across all twelve ordered pairs (Figure 13). Erasing a probability-aligned axis from cross-type embeddings degrades the downstream linear decoder in proportion to the probability content the eraser shares with the target, and this scaling holds across two architecturally distinct models --- a 1024-dimensional BERT-large variant and a 4096-dimensional decoder-derived embedding head. We treat cross-model agreement on this cross-pair signature, rather than per-pair functional verdicts, as the load-bearing finding: the four within-type axes carry probability information that downstream decoders use, and the use is graded by geometric alignment in the way one would predict if the four axes were partially redundant projections of a shared epistemic dimension (§5).

The predicative--modal pair, calibrated to the same Mosteller medians in adjective and adverb form respectively, has the strongest a priori reason to share content; its cosine alignment is the highest of the twelve ordered pairs in both models (\(\cos = 0.88\) on mxbai-embed-large, \(0.79\) on qwen3-embedding). Erasing the predicative axis from modal-type embeddings raises MAE from 6.8 to 25.2 percentage points on mxbai (\(\Delta\mathrm{MAE} = +18.4\)) and from 5.2 to 22.5 on qwen3 (\(+17.4\)); the reverse direction (erase modal, decode with predicative) raises MAE from 4.6 to 29.2 on mxbai (\(+24.6\)) and from 5.5 to 26.0 on qwen3 (\(+20.5\)). We test the headline pair against two complementary nulls that answer different methodological questions. The cosine-matched random-direction null asks whether this \emph{direction} damages more than a random direction with the same geometric overlap with \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_B\); the label-permutation null asks whether the \emph{probability content} of \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_A\) is doing the work, retraining the eraser on shuffled Mosteller medians while holding the template subspace, regularizer, and diff-vector geometry fixed. The headline pair clears both. Real-axis \(\Delta\mathrm{MAE}\) exceeds matched-random direction erasure with ratios of \(1.02\), \(1.12\), \(1.17\), and \(1.23\) across the four model \(\times\) direction combinations (the matched-random control is by construction stringent at high cosine --- at \(\cos = 0.88\) it reproduces approximately 98\% of the real-axis MAE damage by geometric overlap alone, §6 L3 --- which compresses headroom but not interpretability of the ratio). Against the label-permutation null, whose null distribution has substantial variance (\(\sigma\) of \(1.7\) to \(4.3\) percentage points on the headline pair across the four combinations), real \(\Delta\mathrm{MAE}\) exceeds every one of 500 shuffles, \(p = 0.002\) in all four cases (mxbai Pred\(\to\)Modal real \(+18.37\) vs.~null \(+1.22 \pm 1.71\); mxbai Modal\(\to\)Pred real \(+24.62\) vs.~\(+3.27 \pm 4.28\); qwen3 Pred\(\to\)Modal real \(+17.36\) vs.~\(+1.28 \pm 1.87\); qwen3 Modal\(\to\)Pred real \(+20.49\) vs.~\(+2.67 \pm 3.88\)). The label-permutation null compensates directly for the matched-random control's compressed headroom at high cosine: its wider null variance is what tests of probability content rather than geometric overlap should produce, and the headline pair clears both.

We treat MAE rather than \(\rho\) as the load-bearing metric throughout §4.4 because in-sample \(\rho\) already reaches \(\geq 0.95\) across all four within-type axes in both models, leaving rank-based metrics with no headroom to register erasure effects: rank-1 projection compresses magnitudes while preserving order, and Spearman \(\rho\) is insensitive to that compression (§6 L4). The \(\rho\)-only view of the same twelve ordered pairs returns five functional pairs on mxbai and three on qwen3 with zero overlap; the MAE view recovers cross-model agreement, with \(r(\cos, \Delta\mathrm{MAE}) = +0.92\) and \(+0.86\) contrasting with \(r(\cos, \Delta\rho) = -0.72\) and \(+0.24\). The cross-pair pattern under the two nulls is the structural observation that mirrors the cross-model \(r\) signature. On qwen3-embedding, eleven of twelve ordered pairs clear both nulls simultaneously, with the remaining pair (Modal\(\to\)frequency adverb) functional under matched-random and trend-level under label-permutation; on mxbai-embed-large, five of twelve pairs clear both nulls, four are functional under matched-random only, and three are functional under neither. Critically, zero of twelve pairs in either model are functional only under the label-permutation null: it is the more stringent test, and where the two nulls disagree, label-permutation is the more conservative direction. We read this as evidence that the matched-random control's high-cosine over-conservatism (§6 L3) and rank-saturation at small \(n\) (§6 L4) jointly bound per-pair resolution on individual low-cosine pairs, while the cross-pair structural signal --- the \(r \approx 0.9\) scaling and the headline pair's clearance of both nulls in both models --- is robust. The §4.4 result is the embedding-class structural analogue of the activation-steering and representation-patching protocols standard in the decoder-LLM linear-feature literature \citep{ji2025calibrating,marks2023geometry,valois2025frame,lepori2026fantasy}: rank-1 representation-level erasure under a calibration-aware downstream linear decoder plays the role causal intervention plays in token-generating models, with the methodological framing developed in §5 and the necessary ``analogue rather than substitute'' caveat in §6 L3.

\subsection{Robustness: dimensional truncation, novel-phrase generalization, compound composition, bimodality probe}\label{robustness-dimensional-truncation-novel-phrase-generalization-compound-composition-bimodality-probe}

Four robustness probes test the verbal probability axis along axes orthogonal to the Mosteller-Vogel-Wintle calibration: dimensional truncation, novel-phrase generalization, compound-hedge composition, and the bimodal-modifier ``possible'' probe. Each is consistent with the headline within-type and cross-dataset results of §4.1--§4.2 and constrains the interpretation of those results in a different direction.

\textbf{Matryoshka dimensional truncation.} Following the Matryoshka Representation Learning protocol \citep{kusupati2022matryoshka}, we re-extract the within-type axes after truncating each model's pooled embedding to 512, 256, 128, 64, and 32 dimensions and recomputing the difference vectors and ridge axis at each truncated dimensionality. On nomic-embed-text v1.5 (768d, MRL-trained), worst-case LOO \(\rho\) across the four within-type axes drops by only 0.027 at 64 dimensions --- a 12\(\times\) compression that preserves rank-based recovery of the probability axis on every type. Even at 32 dimensions (24\(\times\) compression), the worst-case LOO \(\rho\) drop remains 0.116, with the modal axis actually \emph{improving} slightly (0.948 \(\to\) 0.960). On mxbai-embed-large (1024d, not MRL-trained), the axis is robust to 128 dimensions (8\(\times\)) but degrades at 64 dimensions (worst-case LOO \(\rho\) drop = 0.154), as expected for a model whose loss objective does not enforce nested-prefix sufficiency. Axis-stability cosines between the full-dimensional axis and its truncated counterpart confirm this dichotomy: nomic at 64 dimensions retains cos \(\geq 0.94\) to its full-dimensional axis on every type, mxbai cos \(\geq 0.92\) at 128 but falls to 0.85--0.93 at 32. Figure 5 plots the full LOO \(\rho\) versus dimensionality curve. The MRL-versus-non-MRL contrast is the methodological observation: where a model has been explicitly trained for nested-prefix generality, the verbal probability axis inherits that property without retraining.

The MRL-trained model preserves the axis to 64 dimensions (12\textbackslash times compression); the non-MRL model holds at 128 dimensions.}]{figures/fig5_truncation.pdf}}

The MRL-trained model preserves the axis to 64 dimensions (12\(\times\) compression); the non-MRL model holds at 128 dimensions.}\label{fig:truncation}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Novel-phrase generalization.} The Mosteller calibration covers 53 expressions, none of them informal first-person hedges (``I think,'' ``I believe''), doubt expressions (``I doubt,'' ``I wonder if''), anti-hedges (``obviously,'' ``clearly,'' ``without question''), or constructions outside the survey's vocabulary (``signs point to,'' ``I'd wager,'' ``it stands to reason''). To test whether the trained axes encode probability semantics or only Mosteller-vocabulary lookup, we apply each model's trained axes to a held-out set of 26 such phrases embedded as natural sentences and correlate against author-rated intuition probabilities. Spearman \(\rho\) across the 26 phrases reaches 0.752 on nomic-embed-text v1.5, 0.842 on mxbai-embed-large, 0.831 on nomic v2 MoE, 0.870 on embeddinggemma, and 0.895 on qwen3-embedding; on the ten purely novel phrases (the ``novel'' subset, excluding the informal-hedge and anti-hedge categories), the same correlations rise to 0.796--0.942. The geometry orders informal first-person hedges intuitively (believe \textgreater{} think \textgreater{} imagine \textgreater{} suspect \textgreater{} wonder \textgreater{} doubt \textgreater{} not sure) and correctly assigns sub-50\% probabilities to doubt expressions and high-50s/60s to anti-hedges, with a systematic compression effect --- natural sentence constructions distribute the difference vector across more dimensions than the controlled templates do, attenuating projection magnitudes toward the center while preserving rank order. The author-rated ground truth limits the strength of the calibration claim; the result is informative as evidence that the axis ranks out-of-vocabulary phrases sensibly, not as a calibrated psychometric mapping for those phrases. We make this distinction explicit and treat the §4.5 numbers as evidence of generalization rather than as calibrated-prediction claims (§6 L1).

\textbf{Compound-hedge composition.} Natural language stacks hedge cues --- ``I think it will probably succeed,'' ``It seems fairly likely'' --- and the question is whether the difference vector for a compound hedge equals the sum of its component vectors. On qwen3-embedding and mxbai-embed-large, the cosine between a compound difference vector \(\mathbf{d}_{A+B}\) and its component sum \(\mathbf{d}_A + \mathbf{d}_B\) falls in the range 0.82--0.89 across most compound types (first-person + modal, evidential + modal, attenuator + predicative, double first-person), with a systematic magnitude ratio of approximately 0.75 --- the compound is sub-linear in magnitude but near-linear in direction. Negation is the structural exception: \(\mathbf{d}_{\neg A}\) is near-orthogonal to \(\mathbf{d}_A\) (cos = 0.22 on qwen3-embedding for ``not impossible'' versus ``impossible'') rather than antiparallel, and a follow-up probe (FINDINGS-06) finds that negation acts as a \emph{probability-reflecting} operation --- negating a high-probability word produces a vector aligned with the negation of other high-probability words (\(+0.96\) between ``not likely'' and ``not probable'') but anti-correlated with negations of low-probability words (\(-0.93\) between ``not possible'' and ``not impossible''). Negation is not a single direction in the embedding, but its action on the verbal probability axis is structured: it inverts the projection. This is the geometrically appropriate behavior for a probability-reflecting axis and constrains how a downstream calibrator should handle negated hedges (Figure 11).

Most compounds compose near-linearly (cos \textbackslash geq 0.82); negation (cos = 0.22 on qwen3) is the principled exception.}]{figures/fig11_compound.pdf}}

\textbf{Bimodal-modifier ``possible'' probe.} The Mosteller distribution for ``possible'' is bimodal --- one human cluster reads it as logical possibility (5--10\%), another as reasonable chance (40--50\%) --- and the axis, as the IQR result of §4.7 will show, encodes a single point estimate per expression. We probe whether modifiers can disambiguate this in geometry by embedding ``\{modifier\} possible'' with twelve modifiers spanning low-leaning (``barely,'' ``just barely,'' ``remotely'') to high-leaning (``entirely,'' ``very,'' ``eminently''). On mxbai-embed-large, low-leaning compositions of ``possible'' project to 0.1--13.4\% on the predicative axis and high-leaning compositions to 60.3--74.1\%, a spread of 31.6 percentage points (Spearman \(\rho = 0.893\) between projection and expected probability across the twelve modifiers). On qwen3-embedding the spread is 29.7 percentage points; on nomic-embed-text v1.5 it is 20.0. The geometry traverses the bimodality range when a disambiguating modifier is present even though it cannot represent the bare-``possible'' ambiguity directly. Figure 10 visualizes the spread.

\subsection{Null-hypothesis controls}\label{null-hypothesis-controls}

Three controls (\texttt{experiment\_10\_null\_hypothesis.py}, on nomic-embed-text v1.5) establish that the within-type LOO recovery of §4.1 is in the phrase-to-probability mapping rather than in the protocol or template structure.

\textbf{Permutation test.} Randomly permuting the Mosteller medians among the expressions of each type and rerunning the full ridge-plus-LOO pipeline 1,000 times yields a permuted-LOO-\(\rho\) distribution centered near zero with standard deviation 0.29--0.42 per type. For predicative, frequency-adverb, and noun-phrase axes the real-label LOO \(\rho\) exceeds the 99th percentile of the permuted distribution: predicative real \(\rho = 0.874\) at the 99.7th percentile (\(p = 0.003\)), frequency adverb real \(\rho = 0.923\) at the 100th percentile (\(p < 0.001\)), noun phrase real \(\rho = 0.936\) at the 99.5th percentile (\(p = 0.005\)). The same three larger-\(n\) axes pass the permutation test on three additional architectures (embeddinggemma, nomic v2 MoE, mxbai-embed-large) with \(p \leq 0.029\) on all nine remaining (model \(\times\) type) cells, so the within-type calibration result of §4.1 is not a one-model finding. The modal axis at \(n = 10\) does not reach significance on nomic-embed-text v1.5 (real \(\rho = 0.649\) at the 79.2nd percentile, \(p = 0.21\)): with only ten Mosteller-grounded modal expressions, the permuted distribution has high variance, and a non-trivial fraction of label permutations produces LOO \(\rho\) above 0.6 by chance. Two evidence streams jointly inform our reading of this. First, the modal permutation outcome tracks modal LOO \(\rho\) across the four completed models in a smooth gradient --- embeddinggemma fails at LOO \(\rho = 0.59\) (\(p = 0.22\)), nomic-embed-text v1.5 fails at LOO \(\rho = 0.65\) (\(p = 0.21\)), mxbai-embed-large sits at the threshold boundary at LOO \(\rho = 0.81\) (\(p = 0.054\)), and nomic v2 MoE passes cleanly at LOO \(\rho = 0.92\) (\(p = 0.004\)); the same gradient appears in the random-label control (Test 3) reported below. Second, a multi-\(n\) power analysis on nomic-embed-text v1.5 (\texttt{experiment\_10b}) appends author-estimated modal values to the Mosteller-grounded set and reruns the permutation test at \(n \in \{10, 12, 14, 17\}\): \(p\) collapses three orders of magnitude across \(n = 10 \to 14\), with the threshold for \(p < 0.05\) crossed between \(n = 10\) and \(n = 12\). The author-estimated rows are not psychometrically calibrated and are excluded from any calibration claim; they probe sample-size variation only. Together, these are evidence that the modal permutation result is small-\(n\) and model-sensitive rather than evidence that the modal axis lacks signal --- consistent with the small-\(n\) rank-test regime §6 L4 develops in full. The modal axis is independently validated as functional in §4.4 via the concept-erasure analysis on \(n = 10\), where the cosine-matched random-direction null and the label-permutation null both distinguish it cleanly from a geometric correlate. For the three larger-\(n\) axes, the phrase-to-probability mapping is not a property of the templates.

\textbf{Non-epistemic adjective control.} A grammatically clean control set of thirteen evaluative \emph{that}-complement adjectives (``tragic,'' ``regrettable,'' ``unfortunate,'' ``concerning,'' through ``encouraging,'' ``fortunate,'' and ``wonderful''), placed in the same predicative template and trained against deliberately scrambled arbitrary labels in the 20--80 range --- labels chosen so that they do not track the natural negative-to-positive evaluative valence of the set --- returns LOO \(\rho = -0.41\), well below the real-epistemic predicative LOO \(\rho = 0.874\) and on the opposite side of zero from any null fit. The negative sign is interpretable rather than concerning: the embedding has a real evaluative axis spanning ``tragic'' to ``wonderful,'' ridge regression detects this direction from the difference vectors, and the protocol's LOO predictions therefore track natural evaluative valence rather than the arbitrary labels we trained against. This is consistent with the multiple-axis picture §4.1 already establishes from the PCA finding that PC1 captures syntactic frame and the probability signal lives on PC2: the protocol does not trivially fit any-labels-to-any-grammatical-adjectives in this template, and where the embedding does have a coherent semantic axis aligned with the input set, the protocol surfaces \emph{that} axis rather than the imposed labels. The script's \emph{mixed} set, by contrast, returns LOO \(\rho = 0.69\) and triggers a ``WARNING: Non-epistemic adjectives show some structure'' line in the raw output. The mixed set was constructed at the boundary of epistemic content and includes adjectives like ``expected,'' ``obvious,'' ``documented,'' and ``unprecedented,'' several of which are compositionally near-synonymous with Mosteller items. We retain that warning rather than suppressing it and treat the mixed-set \(\rho = 0.69\) as evidence \emph{for} the geometry's epistemic sensitivity --- the axis picks up residual epistemic loading in items like ``expected'' (\(\approx\) ``probable'') and ``obvious'' (\(\approx\) ``certain''). The evaluative control is the load-bearing comparison.

\textbf{Random-label control.} Drawing labels from Uniform\((0, 100)\) for the real Mosteller expressions and rerunning the ridge-plus-LOO pipeline 1,000 times per type yields a random-label LOO \(\rho\) distribution that matches the real-label LOO \(\rho\) in 6 of 1,000 trials for predicative (\(p = 0.006\)), 0 of 1,000 for frequency adverb (\(p < 0.001\)), and 3 of 1,000 for noun phrase (\(p = 0.003\)). The modal axis at \(n = 10\) matches in 197 of 1,000 trials (\(p = 0.20\)), the same low-power signature as the permutation test above. The signal in the three larger-\(n\) axes is in the phrase-probability mapping the model learned during pretraining, not in the structural properties of the regression.
