\subsection{Negative results}\label{negative-results}

Two informative negatives constrain the interpretation of the verbal probability axis: the IQR result tells us what kind of object the axis is, and the ensemble result tells us that the four within-type axes do not stack into a more accurate combined predictor.

\textbf{Interpretive precision is not in the geometry.} \citet{mosteller1990quantifying} report the inter-quartile range (IQR) of human probability ratings per expression alongside the median; ``possible'' has IQR = 42.7 (P25 = 7.5\%, P75 = 50.2\%, the bimodal distribution probed in §4.5), while ``certain'' has IQR = 1.1. We test whether the embedding geometry encodes this interpretive precision by computing the cross-claim consistency of each expression's difference vector --- its mean pairwise cosine across 15 propositional contents --- and correlating against \(-\)IQR. If the geometry encoded which expressions humans agree about, low-IQR expressions should produce more consistent cross-claim directions. Across four models (mxbai-embed-large, qwen3-embedding, nomic v2 MoE, embeddinggemma) the correlation \(\rho(\text{consistency}, -\text{IQR})\) ranges from \(-0.20\) to \(+0.05\) with \(p > 0.5\) in every case. The geometry encodes a single stable meaning per expression, not the spread of human interpretations of that expression. This is informative for what the verbal probability axis \emph{is}: a point estimator on the population probability mapping, not a representation of the variance of that mapping. A practical calibration system that needs interpretive-precision flags must read them from external psychometric data (the Mosteller IQR column) rather than from the axis. The result is also a constraint on the formal-semantics interpretation in §5: the axis is consistent with treating ``probably,'' ``possibly,'' and their kin as continuous-valued operators on a single probability dimension \citep{lassiter2017graded}, not with treating them as distributional objects encoding rater variance.

\textbf{No ensemble of within-type axes beats the single modal axis on novel phrases.} §4.1 yields four within-type axes per model (predicative, frequency adverb, noun phrase, modal). One natural follow-up --- given that these axes are moderately correlated (cos = 0.41--0.88 within a single model on mxbai; cf.~§5) --- is to combine them into a single ensemble predictor. We tested ridge-regressed linear ensemble, magnitude-weighted average, max-projection routing, calibrated logistic stacking, and a naïve four-axis mean against the modal axis alone on the novel-phrase set of §4.5. No ensemble strategy beats the modal axis alone: on mxbai-embed-large the modal-only MAE is 9.7\%, the best ensemble (linear ridge) reaches 11.4\%, and the oracle that knows the ground truth and picks the best axis per phrase reaches 5.9\%. The pattern repeats on qwen3-embedding (modal 5.9\%, best ensemble 8.3\%, oracle 4.3\%) and embeddinggemma (modal 5.6\%, best ensemble 7.5\%, oracle 4.5\%). The modal axis is within 1--4 percentage points of oracle on every model and is the practical fallback for arbitrary natural hedge phrasings. The ensemble's failure to add value is interpretable: the four axes are not independent measurements of a shared latent quantity but partially redundant projections of one underlying epistemic dimension whose modal-frame instantiation happens to dominate the syntactic distribution of natural hedging.

\section{Discussion}\label{discussion}

The recent linear-feature interpretability literature --- \citet{marks2023geometry}, \citet{burger2024truth}, \citet{yu2025directions}, \citet{ji2025calibrating}, \citet{lepori2026fantasy}, and \citet{valois2025frame} --- has documented calibrated linear structure for graded epistemic properties almost exclusively on decoder LLM internal states: residual streams, late-layer hidden states, and unembedding matrices. In each of these settings the natural protocol for separating a functional concept direction from a merely correlated direction is token-level causal intervention --- activation steering, residual-stream patching, guided decoding --- because the model generates tokens and the consequence of perturbing an internal state can be read off the output distribution. Pretrained pooled sentence embedding models are categorically different objects: they compress an input sentence to a single vector for retrieval or similarity, expose no token-generation pathway, and do not admit the steering-style interventions that ground the decoder-class results. The contribution of this paper is to demonstrate that analogous calibrated linear structure exists in this model class, and that doing so honestly requires two adaptations of the decoder-LLM playbook. The validation method is the first: rank-1 representation-level erasure of \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_A\) from a target type's difference vectors, evaluated against a calibration-aware downstream linear decoder and two complementary nulls --- a cosine-matched random-direction control (testing geometric correlation) and a label-permutation null on the eraser axis's training labels (testing probability content), per §4.4 --- is the embedding-class structural analogue of activation steering. The calibration target is the second: rather than the model-internal LLM-as-a-Judge verbal-uncertainty scores \citet{ji2025calibrating} calibrate to, our axis is calibrated to human psychometric medians from \citet{mosteller1990quantifying} and cross-validated against \citet{vogel2022systematic} and \citet{wintle2019verbal}, datasets that span sixty years of replication on independent populations. We frame the §4.4 result as the model-class analogue of decoder-LLM causal intervention rather than as a substitute for it (§6 L3); what it establishes, in conjunction with the calibration result, is that the empirical phenomenon documented in the decoder-LLM linear-feature literature has a counterpart in pretrained pooled sentence embeddings, validated by the appropriate analogues at every step.

The four within-type axes recovered in §4.1 are not independent measurements but constituent directions in a low-dimensional epistemic subspace. Pairwise cosine alignment between the axes is moderate (cf.~§4.7's mxbai-embed-large range of 0.41--0.88), and the predicative--modal pair --- calibrated to the same Mosteller medians in adjective and adverb form respectively --- is the most aligned in every model tested, with that alignment increasing systematically with model capacity (smaller models near 0.5, mxbai-embed-large at 0.88, qwen3-embedding at 0.79; §4.4 reports the latter two from the post-erasure ridge fit). This pattern parallels \citet{yu2025directions}'s extension of one-dimensional truth directions to multi-dimensional cones in decoder LLMs: the verbal probability ``axis'' is more accurately a low-dimensional subspace whose syntactic-frame instantiations are partially redundant projections of a shared latent epistemic dimension, and larger models develop a more unified probability representation that becomes progressively less entangled with syntactic frame. The §4.4 ΔMAE-cos correlation (\(r = 0.92\) on mxbai-embed-large, \(r = 0.86\) on qwen3-embedding) is the functional confirmation of this subspace structure: the larger the geometric alignment between two within-type axes, the more downstream calibration is lost when one is erased from the other's embeddings. The §4.7 ensemble result reaches the same conclusion from the opposite direction. If the four axes were independent measurements of a shared latent quantity, ensembling them would average out independent noise and improve novel-phrase generalization; instead, no ensemble strategy beats the modal axis alone, and the gap to oracle is small (1--4 percentage points across models). At the dimensionalities tested the four axes have not collapsed into one, but they are organized as partially redundant projections of one underlying epistemic dimension whose modal-frame instantiation happens to dominate the syntactic distribution of natural hedging.

A useful way to read the empirical content of this paper is as evidence that distributional embedding geometry and human probability semantics are convergent measurements of one underlying quantity. Three independently collected psychometric datasets spanning more than fifty years \citep{mosteller1990quantifying,vogel2022systematic,wintle2019verbal}, six pretrained embedding models with different architectures and training procedures, and eight typologically diverse languages all agree on the same continuous probability axis, with cross-dataset \(\rho\) reaching 0.991 (Mosteller\(\to\)Vogel) and 0.967 (Mosteller\(\to\)Wintle), cross-linguistic mean ranking \(|\rho| = 0.928\), and concept-erasure functional confirmation across two architectures. Each instrument is exposed to a different source of measurement noise --- Mosteller's 1990 sample of 238 science writers, Vogel's meta-analytic aggregation across 21 studies, Wintle's 2019 expert-elicitation protocol on \(n \approx 924\), and the architectural and training-data heterogeneity of the embedding models --- and their joint agreement on a common ordering and a common calibration is precisely what one would expect if each were a noisy measurement of a single latent quantity: the communicative probability function that human languages have evolved to express. This perspective, complementary to the standard ``embeddings reflect their training data'' framing, is supplied with measurement-theoretic scaffolding by \citet{schockaert2022formal}'s formal framework for embeddings as epistemic states. The §4.7 IQR negative further sharpens the picture. The geometry encodes a single stable point per expression rather than the spread of human interpretations, which is consistent with treating ``probably,'' ``possibly,'' and their kin as continuous-valued operators on a single probability dimension in the sense of \citet{lassiter2017graded}, and inconsistent with treating them as distributional objects encoding rater variance. The verbal probability axis is, in this sense, a \emph{point estimator} on the population probability mapping --- an object that recovers the central tendency of human verbal-probability semantics without recovering the dispersion. We submit this paper as one step in establishing the convergent-instruments frame empirically; the broader question of how far the frame extends to other graded human-meaningful concepts is the larger program it suggests.

A specific class of applications motivates further attention. Pretrained pooled sentence embedding models are the substrate of contemporary language-constituted agents --- chatbots, scaffolded LLM systems, and the broader class of systems whose primary observation and action channels are linguistic. For such agents, reading off expressed uncertainty in a calibrated form is operationally load-bearing: any agentic protocol that depends on the agent's stated confidence --- honest-activation discipline, calibration audits, theory-of-mind reasoning over an interlocutor's epistemic state --- requires the linguistic encoding of uncertainty to map to numerical probability in a known way. The verbal probability axis recovered in this paper supplies one component of that measurement infrastructure: a way to read the uncertainty an agent expresses through language, calibrated against six decades of human psychometric replication, validated across architectures and languages, and confirmed as functional rather than merely correlated. \citet{schockaert2022formal}'s formal framework for embeddings as epistemic states supplies the conceptual scaffolding under which this reading is well-typed; the present paper supplies the empirical instrument. The strongest near-term applications we anticipate are in \textbf{honest-activation discipline} for scaffolded language-constituted agents (does an agent's expressed uncertainty match its model-internal state?), in \textbf{cross-substrate epistemic-state comparison} (do agents on different model classes encode the same uncertainty when shown the same proposition?), and in \textbf{detection of distributional drift} between expressed and actual confidence. We treat these as the most direct downstream uses of the present work and reserve their development for follow-up.

\section{Limitations}\label{limitations}

We name four limitations the present study does not resolve. Remediation is framed as scope-of-future-work rather than as a flaw in the present claims.

\textbf{(L1) Construct validity: template-only evaluation, author-rated novel phrases.} Every Mosteller, Vogel, and Wintle result reported in §4.1--§4.2, the §4.3 cross-linguistic transfer, and the §4.4 concept-erasure experiment uses three controlled syntactic templates (``It is \{X\} that the experiment will succeed'', and analogues for the four within-type axes). External validity to natural text is therefore an inferential step this paper does not make rigorously. Section 4.5 partially mitigates the concern by showing that the trained axes rank novel non-template phrasings (``I think,'' ``I doubt,'' ``signs point to'') with \(\rho = 0.75\)--\(0.94\) across five models against author-rated intuition probabilities, and §4.6 shows a clean evaluative non-epistemic control returns LOO \(\rho = -0.41\) --- the protocol does not trivially fit arbitrary labels on grammatical adjectives in this template. Two follow-ups would close the gaps together: a corpus study with hedged claims drawn from scientific writing, weather forecasts, or IPCC assessment reports --- domains where verbal probability and numerical probability are paired by editorial convention --- would convert the ranking-preserved claim into a calibration claim on natural text; and a small Prolific re-rating study (\(n \geq 10\) annotators per phrase) on the §4.5 novel phrases would convert the author-rated targets into independent psychometric ratings. Both are reserved for follow-up.

\textbf{(L2) Cross-linguistic results are ranking transfer, not native-speaker calibration.} The eight-language probability values used in §4.3 are constructed translations of English Mosteller equivalents (e.g., Japanese ありそうな paired with Mosteller's ``likely'' \(\to 71.1\%\)) rather than values elicited from native-speaker psychometric surveys in each target language. The ranking correlation we report (mean \(|\rho| = 0.928\)) is a defensible claim. The MAE figures are not directly comparable across languages because the ``expected'' value column is itself a translation artifact, and pragmatic-loaded epistemic markers like Japanese まさか carry contextual implicatures a template-driven evaluation cannot capture (§4.3, Table 3, Japanese modal MAE = 18.1\%). Native-speaker psychometric validation in the eight target languages --- replicating Mosteller's 1990 protocol with locally recruited raters --- is the natural next step and is reserved for follow-up.

\textbf{(L3) Non-causal embedding-class intervention.} The §4.4 concept-erasure experiment establishes that the verbal probability axis is functional in the linear-decoder sense --- the headline predicative \(\leftrightarrow\) modal pair clears two complementary nulls on both tested architectures (a cosine-matched random-direction control and a label-permutation null on the eraser axis's training labels), with cross-pair Pearson \(r(\cos, \Delta\mathrm{MAE}) = 0.92/0.86\) as the structural signature. This is the embedding-class analogue of the activation-steering and representation-patching experiments standard in the decoder-LLM linear-feature literature \citep{ji2025calibrating,lepori2026fantasy,marks2023geometry,valois2025frame}; pretrained pooled sentence embedding models lack a token-generation pathway through which to verify that an intervention changes downstream model output, so representation-level erasure validated by a calibrated downstream linear decoder is the appropriate analogue rather than a substitute. The matched-random control is also stringent at high cosine alignment by construction: at the predicative--modal cosine of 0.88, the matched-random direction reproduces approximately 98\% of the real-axis MAE damage geometrically, compressing the headroom for the real-axis effect to clear \(z = +2\). The headline pair clears this stringent threshold and the wider-variance label-permutation null in all four model \(\times\) direction combinations. Bridging sentence-embedding probes to decoder-LLM behavior --- for example, asking whether the verbal-uncertainty feature \citet{ji2025calibrating} localize in residual streams corresponds, under shared input, to the projection of the same sentence onto the pooled-embedding probability axis --- is a natural follow-up question this paper opens but does not answer.

\textbf{(L4) Small per-type sample sizes saturate \(\rho\)-based metrics; the modal axis is most exposed.} Within-type axis training uses Mosteller-derived sets of \(n = 10\) (modal), 11 (noun phrase), 13 (predicative), and 19 (frequency adverb), and in-sample fit reaches \(\rho \geq 0.95\) on every type for both mxbai-embed-large and qwen3-embedding, leaving rank-based metrics with essentially no headroom to register a functional erasure effect. This is why §4.4 leads with MAE rather than \(\rho\): the \(\rho\)-based view of the concept-erasure results yields 5/12 functional pairs on mxbai vs.~3/12 on qwen3 with zero overlap, which reads as cross-model disagreement and dissolves under MAE. The same regime is visible in the §4.6 modal-axis permutation test, where the cross-model gradient and the multi-\(n\) power-analysis curve jointly support a small-\(n\) + model-sensitive interpretation: the \(p < 0.05\) threshold is crossed between \(n = 10\) and \(n = 12\) when author-estimated modal values are appended to the Mosteller-grounded set (the expanded-set rows probe sample-size variation and are not a calibration claim), and \(p\) tracks modal LOO \(\rho\) from clear failures at LOO \(\rho \approx 0.6\) through a threshold boundary at \(0.81\) to a clean pass at \(0.92\). We treat \(\rho\)-saturation at small \(n\) as a property of the available calibration data --- Mosteller's 53 expressions remain the field standard six decades into this literature --- rather than as a flaw in our extraction method. Modal training is restricted to the ten Mosteller-grounded adverbial expressions; an extension to \(\sim 20\) expressions via native-speaker psychometric replication would alleviate the saturation concern and would also support the L2 cross-linguistic remediation if conducted in multiple languages.

\section{Conclusion}\label{conclusion}

We have shown that pretrained pooled sentence embedding models encode a continuously calibrated verbal probability axis aligned with human psychometric data: a single linear direction recovered within syntactic types from frozen pooled representations, calibrated against \citet{mosteller1990quantifying}, cross-validated against \citet{vogel2022systematic} and \citet{wintle2019verbal}, transferred zero-shot in ranking to eight typologically diverse languages, robust to dimensional truncation, and confirmed as functional rather than merely correlated by representation-level concept erasure under a cosine-matched random-direction control. The result holds across six pretrained embedding models spanning five architectural families and survives three null-hypothesis controls. It establishes for the pretrained pooled sentence embedding class a phenomenon the recent linear-feature interpretability literature has documented for decoder LLM internal states, with representation-level concept erasure standing in for token-level causal intervention and human psychometric data standing in for model-internal calibration targets.

Four directions extend the present work most directly. The first is native-speaker psychometric replication of the Mosteller protocol in the eight target languages of §4.3, which would convert the cross-linguistic ranking-transfer claim into a calibration-transfer claim and resolve the translation-pairing ambiguity §6 L2 names for languages such as Japanese where pragmatic-loaded epistemic markers diverge from English equivalents. The second is real-text corpus evaluation: hedged claims drawn from scientific writing, weather forecasts, and IPCC assessment reports --- domains in which verbal probability and numerical probability are paired by editorial convention --- would convert the template-controlled calibration of §4.1--§4.2 into a calibration claim on natural hedged text and address the external-validity concern of §6 L1. The third is bridging pretrained pooled sentence embedding probes to decoder-LLM internal-state probes by asking whether the verbal-uncertainty feature \citet{ji2025calibrating} localize in residual streams corresponds, under shared input, to the projection of the same sentence onto the pooled-embedding probability axis we recover here; \citeauthor{ji2025calibrating}'s Appendix E.2 already establishes a small bridge of this kind, and a systematic comparison would test whether the two model classes converge on the same epistemic dimension in the sense developed in §5 (cf.~§6 L3). The fourth is enlarging the underlying psychometric calibration corpus --- extending Mosteller's modal subset with native-speaker-validated supplements would alleviate the small-sample saturation §6 L4 imposes on the modal axis. We close on the framing §5 develops: distributional embedding geometry and human psychometric surveys are most usefully read as convergent instruments measuring one underlying quantity, and the present paper is one empirical step toward that frame.
